content.content:
1	# Guide for adding JusPrin tools
2	
3	**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.
4	
5	JusPrin has one tool system. A new capability is defined once, in the shared registry. `ToolExecutionCoordinator` runs it. Its implementation reads and changes the open project through the typed workspace interface. Two adapters, one for OpenAI and one for MCP, only translate that single definition into the format each side expects. The aim of this guide is a tool catalog that stays small, does only what it claims to do, can change safely over time, and is shaped by real printing tasks. It should not be shaped by a list of every feature OrcaSlicer has.
6	
7	Treat this guide as the starting point. Change it when what you learn from implementing, from real MCP clients, or from evals shows that a rule, a contract, a limit, or a sequence here should change. Do not keep a planning assumption just because it is written here. Base every revision on evidence, and describe significant changes in the PR. Two things do not change: OrcaSlicer stays the owner of the state it owns, and the verification requirements stay.
8	
9	Before you touch any OrcaSlicer class that holds live state, read [the production documentation](README.md), [production architecture](architecture.md), and [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md). The current tool definitions are in [`ToolRegistry.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp). The code that runs them is in [`ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp). The code that presents them over MCP is in [`McpProtocol.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp).
10	
11	External clients on the same machine connect through the bundled `jusprin-mcp` stdio helper, which is set up from **Connect AI tools...**. The helper and the server inside the app are compiled from the same registry. So every new tool you offer must have the same catalog entry and the same schema whether the app is running (live) or not (offline), for the same build and the same negotiated protocol version. Do not add a catalog that exists in only one adapter. Connecting to the server directly over HTTP is a route for developers. It is not what the default setup instructions tell people to do.
12	
13	## Words this guide uses
14	
15	- **Registry.** The one list of tool definitions, compiled into the app (`ToolRegistry.cpp`).
16	- **Catalog.** The list of tools as a caller sees it.
17	- **Coordinator.** `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, the class that queues tool calls and runs them on the GUI thread.
18	- **Workspace.** The typed C++ interface (`IWorkspace`) through which JusPrin reads and changes the open project. It has two implementations, called workspace adapters. The real one works on live OrcaSlicer. The fake one is for tests.
19	- **Tool adapter.** Code that translates registry definitions and results for one kind of caller. There are two: the in-app adapter, which uses OpenAI's format and serves the Agent panel, and the MCP adapter, which serves external clients. "Both adapters" in this guide means these two.
20	- **Projection.** The form in which one tool adapter presents a definition or a result.
21	- **Exposure.** The registry setting that says which callers are offered a tool.
22	- **Owner.** The OrcaSlicer class that holds the real copy of some state, or that already implements an operation.
23	- **Seam.** A small addition to a file OrcaSlicer owns, which lets fork code call or observe OrcaSlicer's behavior.
24	- **Session and revision.** `sessionId` identifies the project that is currently open. `revision` is a counter the workspace raises when its state changes. A call that was prepared against an older session or revision is called stale.
25	- **Action class.** Whether a tool is read-only, a mutation (it changes something), or destructive.
26	- **Dirty.** A preset is dirty when it has unsaved edits.
27	- **Eval.** An automated test that gives a model a task and checks the transcript that results.
28	- **M0 to M5.** The milestones in which the tool catalog was delivered.
29	
30	## Current connection and execution boundary
31	
32	- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
33	- The shell tells the server where its discovery file is: `<data_dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`. The running server writes its details there in one atomic step: the actual address, the PID, a unique `instanceId` for this run, the build version, and the protocol versions. Before a server removes the record, it checks, while holding the discovery lock, that the record is its own. An older server therefore cannot remove a newer server's record, even inside the same process. On POSIX systems the file has mode `0600`.
34	- The helper checks that the discovery file is valid, and then tests that the address in it answers. When the app starts or restarts later, the helper follows the new record. The helper never launches JusPrin. The discovery file holds one record, and the last server to write it wins. So the helper works with one selected instance; there is no way to choose among several. `--discovery`, `JUSPRIN_MCP_DISCOVERY`, and `JUSPRIN_MCP_URL` override the file path or the address. They do not switch anything on. The connection entries that Connect writes use `--discovery` with the app's actual data directory.
35	- When the app is not running, the helper answers discovery and tool-list requests from the registry compiled into the helper. Tool calls made while the app is not running return `workspace_unavailable`. When the app can be reached, the helper uses the app's live catalog and results, even when the app and the helper are different versions. Do not replace a live app's tool list with the helper's compiled one. A version difference between the two is logged.
36	- The HTTP adapter accepts MCP protocol version `2026-07-28`. The helper can also negotiate the older versions `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The helper does all conversion between versions. Code that executes a tool must not behave differently for different protocol versions.
37	- **Connect** shows the person the command or the file edit and asks for confirmation first. Then it either runs the Claude Code or Codex CLI, or merges the JusPrin entry into the JSON configuration of Claude Desktop/local Cowork, Cursor or VS Code. A JSON edit keeps unrelated settings and makes a backup. It is refused when the preview is out of date or when the destination is a symlink. It does not protect against another editor writing the same file at the exact moment of replacement.
38	- On macOS the helper is bundled next to the app executable. Windows has a matching install rule. On Linux, the entry for an AppImage uses the installed image's path plus `--mcp-bridge`, and the app handles that flag before the GUI starts. Do not save a temporary AppImage mount path as the command.
39	
40	Workspace commands run on the GUI thread, through the shared coordinator. A timer owned by the shell keeps execution moving, so execution does not depend on the WebView's handshake. No external client ever gets direct access to OrcaSlicer objects.
41	
42	A call from an external client is tagged `ToolSource::Mcp`. The MCP adapter sets that tag, so it can be trusted, and it is kept for the activity history and for diagnostics. External calls run through the same coordinator and the same workspace commands as calls from the in-app Agent. The change log records the edits they make, as it records every edit, and marks them `external`. In the conversation thread those edits appear as rows that say "External tool", where a change made in the app says "Agent".
43	
44	## Start with an eval failure
45	
46	The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.
47	
48	Write down:
49	
50	- what the user wanted to achieve;
51	- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
52	- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
53	- what a successful transcript should look like;
54	- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
55	- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.
56	
57	If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.
58	
59	The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not approve a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.
60	
61	## Decide whether this should be a tool
62	
63	Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.
64	
65	Do not add a tool for:
66	
67	- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
68	- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
69	- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
70	- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
71	- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
72	- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
73	- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.
74	
75	A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.
76	
77	## Skills versus tools
78	
79	A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?
80	
81	- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
82	- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.
83	
84	The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.
85	
86	A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:
87	
88	- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
89	- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
90	- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
91	- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.
92	
93	The file-load instructions (`AgentUI/src/fileReportInstructions.ts`) are a skill that the app inserts into the conversation for one turn. The first message after a file loads is a judgement about the load report. It is not an operation, so it is text. This is the only kind of skill built so far. The other kind would be a skill the model opens by name, after picking it from an index that has one line per skill. Nothing loads skills that way yet. Until something does, a skill is text that the app inserts on a turn where the app already knows the situation.
94	
95	The cases in between:
96	
97	- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
98	- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
99	- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
100	- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.
101	
102	When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.
103	
104	How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.
105	
106	## Prefer extending nouns over multiplying verbs
107	
108	The settings workflow has four operations that do not change. They work on searchable data, whichever preset layer the values belong to:
109	
110	```text
111	settings_search → settings_get → settings_preview_patch → settings_apply_patch
112	```
113	
114	Do not create one tool per setting:
115	
116	```text
117	set_layer_height
118	set_wall_loops
119	set_infill_density
120	set_support_angle
121	```
122	
123	The same rule applies to presets, project objects, plates, warnings, and slice reports. Extend the typed records that describe them, and the size-limited tools that query them, before you create dozens of special-purpose actions.
124	
125	A new operation deserves its own tool when it really differs from the existing ones in at least one of these ways: how it is authorized, whether it applies completely or not at all, how it starts, runs, and ends, or what its result means. `slice_start` is an example. It is not one more way to change settings. It starts OrcaSlicer work that runs in the background, and it completes in a different way from a settings change. That difference justifies a separate tool.
126	
127	Split an operation into a preview tool and an apply tool only where OrcaSlicer may rewrite, replace, or refuse what the caller asked for. In those cases the caller has to see what would really happen before proposing the change. There are four such cases:
128	
129	- settings, because OrcaSlicer's normalizer (the code that adjusts dependent settings after an edit) can rewrite values;
130	- preset selection, because OrcaSlicer may substitute a compatible preset, and dirty edits may be lost;
131	- topology changes such as cutting, splitting, or merging, because the caller needs to see the resulting pieces;
132	- preflight (the check before a print is sent), because of filament mapping and printer readiness.
133	
134	Everywhere else, the coordinator computes and validates the resulting state as part of the call. If a preview would only repeat its input back, do not make it a tool.
135	
136	Prefer read tools whose results have a fixed, typed shape. Avoid one general record search whose result changes shape. Each section of `workspace_inspect` keeps its own fixed shape. A generic `records_search` whose result shape depends on a `kind` argument would make the model guess what comes back.
137	
138	## Tool budget and tool shape
139	
140	The limit on the number of tools comes from how much the model has to load on each turn. It does not come from how much the app can do. The rules in this section rest on this evidence:
141	
142	- OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest.
143	- Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools aimed at high-impact workflows. It names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error.
144	- A [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured three interfaces. A generic interface of thin tools scored below raw SQL. Tools shaped around the domain scored far above both.
145	- The "god tool", one tool that dispatches many unrelated actions through a single `action` parameter, is a documented anti-pattern.
146	
147	The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, and two thirds of that is output schema.
148	
149	**How tools are loaded for now.** Both adapters load every registered tool on every turn. The in-app adapter sends the full function list with each request, and MCP `tools/list` returns the whole catalog. This is the simplest behaviour that is correct. It also keeps the tools array byte-identical through a chat, and OpenAI's prompt cache depends on exactly that. The budget is 20 definitions per turn. Going over 20 does not block anything. It is the point at which we start watching the measurements. The live regression test records definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for each request. The journey catalog below goes over 20 definitions from its first milestone. We accept that until those measurements show the model selecting wrong tools or running short of context.
150	
151	**The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.**
152	
153	| After milestone | In-app definitions | In-app bytes | MCP definitions | MCP bytes | MCP bytes through the offline helper recipe |
154	|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
155	| M0 | 7 | 3,145 | 5 | 3,147 | |
156	| M1 | 11 | 6,482 | 9 | 6,915 | |
157	| M2 | 18 | 12,721 | 16 | 13,911 | 13,894 |
158	| M3 | 20 | 19,331 | 21 | 22,661 | 22,639 |
159	| M4 | 20 | 21,594 | 21 | 24,923 | 24,901 |
160	| M5 | 25 | 29,148 | 26 | 33,013 | |
161	
162	The M5 figure for MCP was read over two `tools/list` pages.
163	
164	The `--live-agent` regression test, run at M0 and at M1, shows what those definitions cost in tokens. The first request of a conversation gets nothing from the cache and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0 and 1,733 at M1. So four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, paid once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (at M1, 5,864 input tokens, of which 5,376 were cached). That is because the tools array is byte-identical through a chat, and the cache depends on that. At M2, the same test made eleven requests that took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens, with 42 to 91 per cent cached. None of the eleven started with an empty cache, because an earlier run on the same day had already cached the shared beginning of the prompt. So that run did not measure the uncached cost at M2.
165	
166	The conclusion is that a definition adds cost to the *first* request of each conversation, not to every turn. That is why going over the budget only makes us look at the measurements and does not block a tool. Two things would change this conclusion: a catalog so large that the first request of every conversation is expensive by itself, or transcripts that show the model choosing the wrong tool. Watch for both. Neither has appeared yet.
167	
168	**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.
169	
170	What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:
171	
172	- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
173	- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one.
174	- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.
175	- The settings tools are allowed only with `scope: "printer"`, on the printer the conversation is about.
176	
177	A Change conversation may be about a stock profile (one that ships with OrcaSlicer) that the project has selected. That happens when the person chooses Printer settings… in the header on a project that uses a stock profile. In that case, changes to the nozzle and to the connection are refused with `stock_profile`. Changes to settings are saved as a copy of the profile, and the conversation follows that copy from then on (`PrinterConversation::tool_settled`). A Change conversation is never turned into an Add conversation. The code that opens a Change conversation checks that the printer is there, and shows OrcaSlicer's error dialog when it is not.
178	
179	The header's filament chat uses the same panel (`PrinterPanel::open_filament`). It is offered the four settings tools and nothing else, and it gets no project state. It has its own instructions. The page writes them in `AgentUI/src/filamentInstructions.ts` and sends them with `filament_instructions`. The page writes them from the facts the app sends as the session part of the panel's state (`PrinterPanel::filament_session_json`): the preset's name, its slot and material, and, for a stock filament, the copy that a change is saved as. The preflight check for this chat allows the settings tools only with `scope: "filament"` on that preset. It refuses an apply that has no `persistAs`, with `not_saved`, because the chat is gone when it closes. When a copy is saved in the preset's place, the chat is about that copy from then on, and the page writes the instructions again for the copy. Until 2026-09-29 the filament chat ran on the project assistant's instructions and tools. With those, the model read "make the nozzle 5 degrees hotter" as a request to print. In another run it set 205 °C when the value was 220 °C, without reading the value first.
180	
181	We do not give each mode a different tool list, for two reasons. The conversation has to refuse disallowed calls anyway, whatever list the model is shown. And the way to restrict tools while keeping the list stable (`tool_choice` with `allowed_tools`) exists only on some providers. We would reconsider if transcripts showed the model reaching for a refused tool and then failing to recover. `tests/printer_prompt` measures this with the `change-add-another` case.
182	
183	Two past changes explain the current design:
184	
185	- Until 2026-09-23 the panel offered one tool per mode (7f66e75b07). The reason was to keep a printer lookup from clearing the pinned card of the printer a Change session was about. That card is gone (4d4f9e466b). Offering one tool per step also left an Add conversation with no tool to connect the printer it had just added (8334b3395b).
186	- On 2026-09-28 three tools were removed (b60fc2d8e6): `printer_manual_setup`, `printer_manual_connection` and `printer_setup_finish`. These were the tools that opened a window or closed the panel. OrcaSlicer's full printer list and a printer's settings are still reachable from the panel's own buttons, and the person closes the panel.
187	
188	The app decides which tools are offered. The page writes the text: `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts` holds the instructions, and `AgentUI/src/printerWords.ts` holds the notes the model reads after a tap. If a turn arrives before the page has written its instructions, the app refuses the turn. It does not send the turn with the project assistant's prompt. The instructions for an Add conversation carry the whole printer list, about 28 KB. That text is always the same and sits at the start of the instructions, so it is cached. No printer conversation carries the project: no workspace state goes into the turn, and none goes into a tool result.
189	
190	**Deferral, when the measurements say so.** Deferral means the model first sees only a short index and loads a tool's full definition when it needs it. Use the deferral feature that the model platform provides. Never write our own mechanism for switching tools in and out. For the in-app Agent, the platform feature is OpenAI's `tool_search` with `defer_loading: true` on the Responses API. It is documented for `gpt-5.4` and later. Whether it works on the pinned `gpt-5.4-mini` has not been verified. On the MCP side, clients defer by themselves, as Claude Code does. Tools would be deferred one toolset at a time (toolsets are the named groups in the candidate catalog), and OpenAI recommends fewer than ten functions per namespace. Do not build a tool that enables a toolset by rewriting the tools array. Every switch would break the prompt cache.
191	
192	**Shape each tool as a domain operation.** A tool does one thing that a slicer user has a name for: place an object, lay out the plates, mark a region, set up the printer. Do not wrap each OrcaSlicer function in its own tool. Do not build a tool that interprets a list of unrelated commands. One operation may have several optional facets, as long as each facet has its own type and the tool rejects facets that conflict.
193	
194	**Batch only where items share a shape.** Good examples are a list of setting changes, a list of intent fields, a list of annotations, and a list of layout rows with one row per object. A list that mixes transforms, imports, and deletes is the god tool described above. It is refused.
195	
196	**Fold reads into sections and detail levels before adding a read tool.** A new read tool is justified in only two cases. Either its inputs are of a different kind (a search over a large catalog, an analysis of one object, a report on a sliced plate), or its result is an image.
197	
198	**Let call logs decide consolidation.** If transcripts show that two tools are always called together, consider merging them. If two facets of one tool are never used together, consider splitting them. Make these decisions from eval evidence, not from a design discussion.
199	
200	**Output schemas are not advertised over MCP.** No client was shown to use them, and they were two thirds of the catalog. `tools/list` no longer carries `outputSchema`. `validate_output` still checks every successful MCP result, so a result that breaks its contract still fails with a visible error. We measured the effect on one build, with the recipe near the end of this guide. With five tools, the catalog went from 9,723 bytes to 3,141, which is from about 2,430 tokens to 785. Only the MCP side saves anything. The in-app adapter has always sent `input_schema` as `parameters` and nothing else, so an in-app turn never carried output schemas. Restore the field only for a client that is shown to read it.
201	
202	## Choose the narrowest honest scope
203	
204	Do not put an enum value in a schema, such as one of `printer | filament | process | object`, unless every advertised value works in both the fake and the real workspace adapter and inherits values the way the documentation says.
205	
206	For each proposed capability, answer:
207	
208	1. Which OrcaSlicer owner holds the real state or performs the operation?
209	2. Is the command valid for the whole project, one plate, one object, one instance, or one preset layer?
210	3. What stable ID identifies the target, and when does that ID expire?
211	4. Which revision must still be current when the command executes?
212	5. Which existing OrcaSlicer undo snapshot covers the change, and how is the change undone, reset, or reverted? Or does ordinary project Undo not apply?
213	6. Which workspace change reasons tell readers that they must read again?
214	7. What happens if the user edits something in the GUI while the call is queued or running?
215	
216	If any of these answers is unclear, the tool's contract is not ready.
217	
218	## Reuse the one authority path
219	
220	Every change to the project must take this route:
221	
222	```text
223	adapter call
224	→ shared registry validation
225	→ ToolExecutionCoordinator queue
226	→ immediate execution
227	→ IWorkspace command
228	→ current Orca owner
229	→ Orca history and state change
230	→ coalesced workspace event
231	→ fresh snapshot/result
232	```
233	
234	A tool adapter must not call `Plater`, `Model`, `PresetBundle`, wxWidgets, or slicing objects directly. Do not copy an OrcaSlicer operation into JusPrin. If the operation you need exists only inside OrcaSlicer's UI code, add the smallest possible seam to the class that currently owns the operation. Name the seam for what it does, and put nothing JusPrin-specific in it.
235	
236	Any change to a file OrcaSlicer owns must follow [fork stewardship](fork-stewardship.md). Keep the diff small, and add lines instead of rewriting existing ones. Record why the seam belongs where you put it, identify the upstream lines you touched, and include the rebase evidence.
237	
238	## JusPrin-owned project state
239	
240	Some product state is not held anywhere in OrcaSlicer: the print intent, the pinned agent plan, semantic region annotations, physical facts the user confirmed about a printer, and the monitoring policy that authorizes automatic pausing. For this state, the "current Orca owner" step in the route above is a JusPrin store instead. Every other step stays the same. The rules are:
241	
242	- **Storage.** State that belongs to a project (intent, plan, regions, conversation, and attachments) lives in the local project store, under a project ID that does not change. The current `ProjectStateDocument` is saved separately from model checkpoints. An imported project may contain the older `Auxiliaries/JusPrin/state.json` and its recovery mirror. Those are read only to migrate them. Three things remain fields of that document:
243	  - the print intent, `printIntent`. A write inserts or updates one field by name, and each field carries its provenance;
244	  - the plan, `plan`. A write replaces the whole plan;
245	  - the region annotations, `regions`. A write replaces the whole list, and each record is stamped with a seq when it changes.
246	
247	  State that belongs to a printer (confirmed facts, monitoring policy) stays in app data, stored per printer identity, the way `PrinterFactsStore` keeps it. Confirmed facts carry an expiry, because the physical world changes without telling the app. See [Local autosave and version history](autosave-version-history.md).
248	- **Revision.** Every write has to signal that it happened, so that readers read again. Two questions are still **open**: which signal to use, and whether the signal invalidates actions that are already queued. They belong to the milestone that adds the first writer. The obvious answer would be to publish a `WorkspaceChangeReasons` bit and add that bit to `kInvalidatingReasons`. That cannot be built as described. `settings_apply_patch` requires its caller's `expectedRevision` to equal the current revision exactly. So if the revision goes up at any point between a client's preview and its apply, the apply fails as `stale_workspace`. An agent that recorded its plan between previewing and applying would make its own call fail. There is an existing example of the alternative: the edit feed (`WorkspaceEditHub`) reports a change without raising the revision. Decide separately for each kind of state. A region annotation generates OrcaSlicer artifacts, so it is a real change to the project. An answer about intent, or a statement of the plan, is not. In the code as built, writing a region record signals nothing by itself. The artifacts it generates are ordinary OrcaSlicer edits, and they raise the revision in the usual way. So an action that was queued before an annotation goes stale, exactly as it would after any other edit to the model.
249	- **Undo.** None of this state is in OrcaSlicer's undo stack. Results say `projectUndo: false`. Region annotations are the awkward case. They generate OrcaSlicer artifacts (modifier volumes, enforcers, blockers, paint), and those artifacts *are* in the undo stack. So project Undo can leave an annotation without its artifacts, or leave an artifact without its annotation. The `regions` section of `object_analyze` reports both situations, and `region_annotate` generates the artifacts again. The result of a place, divide, or repair lists the regions whose link to the geometry that operation broke.
250	- **Provenance (where a value came from).** Any field that records a fact about the world or about what the user wants also records its source: `file` (read from the project or a profile), `observed` (reported by a sensor or the printer, with a timestamp), `agent_inferred`, or `user_confirmed`. A tool marks a value `user_confirmed` only when the call is based on something the user explicitly said. Values the agent inferred stay `agent_inferred`. When a tool reads printer state, it reports the `configured` value and the `observed` value of the same fact separately, and it computes the `mismatches` between them itself. That comparison is not left to the model.
251	
252	## Define the contract before the implementation
253	
254	For every new tool, the registry entry, together with its contract and tests, must specify:
255	
256	- a name that will not change, in lowercase with underscores;
257	- a short title, shown in the activity UI;
258	- a short description that says when to use the tool;
259	- a strict JSON Schema for the input, with `additionalProperties: false` where practical;
260	- a JSON Schema for the output;
261	- its `ActionClass`, which is trusted because it is set in the registry;
262	- whether it is offered to the in-app Agent, to MCP, or to both;
263	- what must be true for it to be available, such as an open FFF project (FFF is ordinary filament printing) or a selected object;
264	- whether the action is revision-sensitive, meaning it must fail when the workspace has changed since it was requested;
265	- whether it applies completely or not at all, and how it is really undone, reset, or reverted. Say so explicitly when normal project Undo does not apply;
266	- what happens when it is cancelled;
267	- the size limits on its output and how results are paged; and
268	- its errors, as structured codes that are specific to the task.
269	
270	The registry cannot change while the app runs, and its entries always come in the same order. A tool adapter may leave tools out, based on the exposure each tool declares. An adapter must not change a tool's action class, validation, or behavior. Keep the list that MCP clients see stable. The only exception would be a server that also implements and tests the current protocol's notification for a changed tool list. When a tool cannot run because of the app's current state, report that from `tools/call` instead of removing the tool from the list.
271	
272	`ToolDefinition` currently stores the name, title, description, input and output schemas, action class, exposure, availability, and handler. The other properties are not registry fields. Whether a tool is revision-sensitive, whether it is all-or-nothing, how it cancels, and how it appears in history are all determined by the coordinator and workspace code, and checked by their tests. `ToolAvailability` currently describes the request a tool is called from (`Always` or `ImportableAttachment`). It does not filter tools by the current state of the project.
273	
274	Inputs are validated by the `valid_arguments` decoder that the registry has for each handler. Changing only the JSON Schema does not change which calls are accepted. Successful MCP output is checked by `validate_output`, which deliberately understands only a small set of schema keywords. Before you use a keyword it does not support, extend the validator and add tests. Do not assume that `validate_output` implements all of JSON Schema, or that every adapter validates output automatically.
275	
276	### Naming and compatibility
277	
278	- Prefer names such as `slice_start` and `presets_compare`.
279	- Do not rename a released tool without a strong reason. Treat names and schemas as public APIs.
280	- Add optional fields in a way that keeps existing callers working. Do not change the meaning or the type of an existing field.
281	- When a breaking change to a contract cannot be avoided, add a versioned replacement. Stop advertising the old definition after a documented migration period, and keep a targeted compatibility test for as long as both exist.
282	- Use one canonical name for a tool in every adapter. Do not keep separate OpenAI and MCP aliases unless a defect in a client is documented and tested.
283	
284	## Input design
285	
286	A tool's inputs should say what the caller wants and which thing it wants it done to. They should not describe how the request is transported or how the UI works.
287	
288	- Send OrcaSlicer IDs as JSON strings, so that the full width of the native ID is preserved.
289	- Use canonical setting keys, and values in their normalized form.
290	- The first catalog had three in-app fixtures: `duplicate_object`, `import_model`, and `inspect_selection`. All three are retired. `plate_layout` replaced the first, `object_import` replaced the second, and the selection ids in the summary of `workspace_inspect` replaced the third. When the coordinator queues an action, it records the session and the revision. It invalidates queued actions when a relevant workspace event arrives, and it checks again before executing. A change to the selection alone does not invalidate an action that is aimed at a specific object, and does not redirect it.
291	- Some new operations read a value, change it, and write it back, and must detect anything that changed since the caller's earlier read. For such an operation, design explicit inputs for the expected session and revision in its own schema and decoder, and test them. A check made when the call is proposed does not prove that the caller's earlier read is still current. Do not quietly add required arguments to tools that already exist.
292	- Put changes that must succeed or fail together into one call.
293	- Make the caller say which thing it means. Do not fall back to a hidden default. The exception is a tool whose name clearly promises the current selection or the active plate.
294	- Reject unknown fields. Reject inputs that select the target in conflicting ways.
295	- A caller may pass a filesystem path only to a tool that does three things: it validates the exact absolute path, it restricts what kind of file the path may be and where, and it documents whether it reads, creates, or overwrites. The candidate catalog has three such tools: `object_import_file`, `project_open`, and `export_file`. No read-only tool accepts a path. In-app clients keep using attachments, which need no path.
296	- Do not make the model repeat data that the server can read for itself, from the real source, when the call executes.
297	- Do not put a large catalog into a schema as an enum. Offer a size-limited search and a way to fetch details instead.
298	
299	**One exception, with its evidence: the printer list.** Working out which printer someone means from what they say takes the model's understanding. It is not a lookup. A search tool placed in front of the model did the job badly. `printer_catalog_search` required every word of the query to appear in a model's name, and it returned the first few matches in file order. As a result "voron 2.4 350mm" came back unsupported, "x1c" matched another manufacturer's printer, and "prusa" showed three of thirteen.
300	
301	So the instructions for an Add session now carry every printer the panel offers, one per line, in the form `<catalogId> | <brand> <model> | <build volume>`. There are 383 lines. They come from `PrinterCatalog::panel_printers`, are sent to the page as the session's `context`, and are written into the instructions by `AgentUI/src/printerInstructions.ts`. `printer_identify` checks the ids that the model copies from the list.
302	
303	This was measured on 2026-09-18, through the app's own request and tool results, on `gpt-5.4-mini`, with three runs of each case:
304	
305	- the word test set: 138/150;
306	- the photo test set: 29/45;
307	- the handoff's own cases, with those four queries among them: 21/21.
308	
309	The model tried 33 times to show more than three printers. Each attempt was refused with `too_many`, and the model then asked a question to narrow the choice. So no answer ever showed three of many. Two weak spots remain. One is a query that equals one model's name and is also the beginning of other models' names ("bambu a1": 0/3). The other is a photo with no readable name. The test sets and the runner are in `agent-docs/jusprin/spikes/printer-identify/`, which is uncommitted and sits beside the earlier spikes.
310	
311	The list is always the same text at the start of the instructions, so it is cached. This approach is right only while the list stays at a few hundred lines.
312	
313	The coordinator looks up the action class and the handler from the tool's name. Never accept either one from the call's arguments.
314	
315	## Output design
316	
317	Decide how large a response may be before you add fields to it. A full project tree, every setting definition, G-code statistics for every layer, or an unlimited list of warnings can each use more of the model's context than the entire tool catalog.
318	
319	Every read tool should use one or more of:
320	
321	- a level of detail (concise, default, or detail);
322	- explicit field selection;
323	- paging, with results always in the same order;
324	- a fixed maximum number of items;
325	- a summary first, followed by separate calls for the details the caller wants; or
326	- an explicit `truncated` flag and a cursor for fetching the rest.
327	
328	A new tool that returns live state should include `sessionId` and `revision` when later calls need them to identify the project and to check that nothing has changed. `workspace_inspect` returns both, and returns the selection as ids. Results that are internal history records have their own schemas. MCP activity results also carry the action ID, the current session, and the current revision in `_meta["io.jusprin/activity"]`. When an event says that state changed, fetch a fresh snapshot. Never treat the event itself as the new state.
329	
330	A successful MCP result contains `structuredContent` that is valid against the output schema, plus a text block that holds the same result serialized as text. An error uses the shared `{error: {code, message, details}}` envelope with `isError: true`. It does not use the success schema.
331	
332	The bridge adjusts results for older clients:
333	
334	- For legacy clients, it removes the result and cache fields that exist only in the modern protocol.
335	- For `2025-03-26`, it also leaves out `structuredContent`, and leaves `outputSchema` and `title` out of the catalog. The serialized text result is kept.
336	- For the later supported revisions, `structuredContent` and `title` are kept.
337	
338	No negotiated version advertises `outputSchema` any more (see [tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). The bridge still has its own code that strips the field, because the bridge also forwards catalogs from a live app of another version. These adjustments are deliberate, for compatibility. They are not conflicting definitions of the same tool.
339	
340	### Image results
341	
342	Three read tools in the candidate catalog return a picture: `project_attachment_read` (a reference image), `view_render` (the prepared or sliced scene), and `printer_camera_snapshot`. The result that the registry produces holds the encoded image and a structured block that describes it (dimensions, camera or layer range, capture time). Each adapter then presents that one result in its own format:
343	
344	- MCP: an `image` content block next to the text and the structured result. `2025-03-26` gets the same block, because image content is older than structured content.
345	- OpenAI: the text and the structured block are the function result. The image is appended as an image input in the continuation, because a function result can only be text.
346	
347	The two adapters present the same result in different formats. The tool itself does not behave differently. Both projections must be tested before the first tool that returns an image ships. Limit every image to 1280 pixels on the long edge and to 2 MB, so that one frame never takes up most of the context window. Never return an image the user has not allowed. A camera frame requires the privacy grant in Printer Configuration. Without it, the call fails with `camera_disabled`.
348	
349	## Errors should teach the next valid call
350	
351	When an invalid state is expected, handle it with ordinary control flow and return a structured error. Do not throw an exception. An error should say what the problem is and include only the data the Agent needs to correct the call.
352	
353	The MCP errors today include `invalid_arguments`, `cancelled`, `workspace_unavailable` and `stale_workspace`. The MCP adapter converts the app's native `stale_revision` and `stale_id` into `stale_workspace`, with the expected and the current session and revision in the details. It converts `unavailable_operation` into `workspace_unavailable`. Protocol errors at the transport level are separate JSON-RPC errors. Native error codes and MCP error codes do not have to be spelled the same.
354	
355	The settings tools return these correction details, each limited in size:
356	
357	- unknown setting: the canonical code `unknown_setting`, the original key, and a short `suggestions` list;
358	- invalid enum value: the key, a diagnostic message, and the valid values in `allowed`;
359	- value out of range: the key, a diagnostic message, and the `min`/`max` bounds. Units are available from the setting's metadata;
360	- incompatible settings: the keys that conflict, and OrcaSlicer's reason;
361	- stale call: the expected and the current session/revision, plus an instruction to read again;
362	- unavailable operation: the requested scope has no active preset or target.
363	
364	A failure that should be impossible (a broken invariant) must stay visible to diagnostics and to Sentry. Catch an error at the boundary between two layers only to recover from it, to translate a known error, or to add context that is essential.
365	
366	## Read, mutation, and destructive policy
367	
368	Decide what a tool may do from its action class in the registry, not from its name:
369	
370	- **Read-only:** cannot change the project, a preset, anything on disk, the printer, or any product state that is saved.
371	- **Mutation:** changes the project, a preset, or saved product state.
372	- **Destructive:** may delete, overwrite, discard, print, export, or restore history.
373	
374	The action class is information used for UI wording, MCP annotations, staleness checks, and the audit history. A valid tool call starts as soon as it has been validated. A tool that previews changes counts as read-only only if tests against both the fake and the real workspace adapter prove that it does none of these: make a preset dirty, raise the workspace revision, create history, cancel slicing, or write a file.
375	
376	## Asynchronous operations
377	
378	Make a tool asynchronous only when the real OrcaSlicer operation is asynchronous. Do not build a second engine for running jobs.
379	
380	Slicing, and any long-running action added later, works like this:
381	
382	1. The workspace command starts the work through its current OrcaSlicer owner and returns a stable action handle.
383	2. `ToolActivity` records that the action is running, and then its final state, with a limited amount of progress information.
384	3. When OrcaSlicer completes or fails, the workspace state advances or is invalidated.
385	4. After that event, the caller fetches the real slice report or the error.
386	5. Cancelling calls OrcaSlicer's real cancellation path, and reports whether the cancellation took effect before the work finished.
387	
388	MCP progress notifications are optional. They belong to one request and exist only to show progress. The progress value must never go backwards, and a client must always have another way to learn the final result. Add the MCP Tasks extension only when a real client or eval needs durable calls that outlive one request. An operation taking several seconds is not enough reason.
389	
390	The current coordinator runs an action in steps, on GUI ticks. It does not provide durable asynchronous jobs. The bridge accepts `notifications/cancelled` in both the legacy and the modern protocol versions. On receiving one, it closes the connection it was forwarding and suppresses any further output for that request. End of input (EOF) ends the bridge session. If the connection is lost before the final response, the client gets `connection_lost` with an **unknown outcome** warning. That is not proof that the mutation was cancelled. Never retry a mutation automatically after such a loss. Read the real state first.
391	
392	## Tool exposure
393	
394	By default, offer a tool through both adapters when both can supply the same inputs. Offer it through only one when the two sides get their context in different ways. The current cases:
395	
396	- `workspace_inspect` is offered through both adapters. Either side can then get the identity of a newly completed slice after slicing, without relying on the context it was given at the start of the turn.
397	- Import from an attachment (`object_import`) is in-app only, and import from a path (`object_import_file`) is MCP only. In the first case the file reaches the app through the conversation. In the second it arrives as an explicit path. These are two separate definitions that each say exactly what they do, both built on one workspace command. They are not one tool that behaves differently for different callers.
398	- `intent_update` and `plan_set` are in-app only. The intent record and the pinned plan belong to the in-app chat. An external agent keeps what its user said, and its own plan, in its own conversation. MCP clients can still read both through `workspace_inspect` and `slice_report`. For the same reason, the in-app assistant's print guidance (`kPrintJourneyGuidance`), which names these tools, is not part of the MCP server's instructions.
399	- A future MCP diagnostics tool may be MCP only, if its purpose is to establish the external connection.
400	- The printer panel's five own tools carry only the `Printer` exposure. Neither adapter lists them. The panel's conversation offers all of them in every mode and refuses the calls that do not fit the conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). What the model reads back from one of these tools is the tool's own result. It is not wrapped in the host's workspace envelope.
401	
402	Write the reason for a restricted exposure next to the registry definition, and test it. Do not use exposure to make one tool behave differently for different callers. If two adapters need different behavior, either improve the shared command or create two separate definitions that each say what they really do.
403	
404	## When resources or skills are appropriate
405	
406	Do not make anything depend on MCP resources until the clients we intend to support have shown that their models fetch resources reliably. A tool that returns a size-limited amount of data is what every client can be expected to handle. Resources may be added as an optional second way to get data that is large, readable, and stable.
407	
408	Keep printing playbooks as skills the model can read (see [Skills versus tools](#skills-versus-tools)). Examples are reducing stringing, improving strength, and choosing a support strategy. Turn a workflow into an executable tool only when it corresponds to a named OrcaSlicer operation that always behaves the same way and has defined inputs, outputs, validation, and behavior for undo, reset, and cancellation. If many step-by-step workflows eventually qualify, build one workflow registry that the model can search, in preference to dozens of nearly identical tool definitions.
409	
410	## Required implementation sequence for one new tool
411	
412	1. Add or update the failing eval and the expected transcript.
413	2. Find the real OrcaSlicer owner. Record how it behaves: object lifetimes, threading, undo history, and events.
414	3. Define the typed inputs, outputs, and errors of the workspace command.
415	4. Implement the command in the fake workspace adapter, and write the workspace contract tests.
416	5. Implement the command in the real workspace adapter, through the smallest possible seam in the owner.
417	6. Prove that making the edit directly in the GUI and making it through the tool leave the same observable state.
418	7. Add the registry definition, the decoder and validator, the link to the code that executes the tool, and the output schema.
419	8. Add coordinator tests for action class, staleness, all-or-nothing behavior, cancellation, and the final activity state.
420	9. Add projection tests for every adapter that offers the tool.
