618	4. An edit at the same time: the user changes a setting in the GUI before an external agent's apply executes. The apply fails as stale, and the agent recovers with one preview and one apply. Applies to every toolset.
619	5. Measuring the load: for the full catalog, the live regression test reports definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for each request, and the transcript is reviewed for cases where the model selected the wrong tool. These numbers decide whether deferral is adopted.
620	
621	## Settings tools: contract and hazards
622	
623	The settings tools are the worked example of everything in this guide. This
624	section records the parts of their design that stay true now that the work is
625	done. The implementation handoff that produced them is retired. Read this
626	section again before you add keys to a write allowlist (the list of settings
627	a tool may change), and before you add any tool that changes a preset.
628	
629	### Standing decisions
630	
631	1. Settings are data. There are four generic tools that work on searchable
632	   records. There is never one tool per setting.
633	2. Every settings call requires `scope`. Its enum is exactly `process`,
634	   `object`, `filament`, or `printer`. A call without `scope` fails with
635	   `invalid_arguments`. There is no default, the scope is never inferred from
636	   `target`, and there is no alias and no compatibility mode.
637	3. What `target` must be depends on the scope, and no other forms are
638	   accepted:
639	
640	   | `scope` | `target` | Meaning |
641	   |---|---|---|
642	   | `process` | forbidden | the active edited FFF process preset |
643	   | `object` | required `{objectId}` | that object's `ModelConfig` overrides |
644	   | `filament` | required `{preset}` | that filament preset, by name |
645	   | `printer` | required `{preset}` | that printer preset, by name |
646	
647	   These rules apply to `settings_search`, `settings_get`,
648	   `settings_preview_patch`, and `settings_apply_patch`. A target that is
649	   extra, missing, empty, or of the wrong shape fails with
650	   `invalid_arguments`.
651	
652	   A preset is named the way OrcaSlicer keys it: by its name, which is unique
653	   within its own collection. `Preset.hpp` says: "The preset name shall be
654	   unique across a single PresetCollection". Never name a preset by the label
655	   a menu shows. The header shows a stock printer's model, and
656	   `Preset::label` puts `"* "` in front of a preset with unsaved edits. Never
657	   name a preset by an alias either. If no visible preset has the given name,
658	   the call fails with `unknown_preset`, and the suggestions are the
659	   project's filaments or the printer in use.
660	
661	   History: the first draft of this contract named a filament by its 1-based
662	   project slot, and edited only the selected printer. On 2026-09-29 Kenneth
663	   chose the preset's name for both. With names, a chat opened for one preset
664	   can change that preset, and a saved printer the project does not use can
665	   be changed, without selecting anything first.
666	4. The scope says which preset or object the settings belong to. It does not
667	   select anything. `printer_setup` remains the only tool that picks the
668	   project's printer, process, or filament. A settings call never discards
669	   dirty edits, never changes nozzle topology (how many nozzles there are and
670	   of what kind), and never substitutes a compatible profile. A settings call
671	   selects a preset only in the two places where OrcaSlicer's own Save or
672	   edit code does. First, a copy saved with `persistAs` takes the original's
673	   place. Second, a filament that is not the one open in its tab is opened
674	   there, the way the sidebar's edit button opens it
675	   (`PlaterPresetComboBox::switch_to_tab`).
676	5. Metadata, parsing, and serialization all come from OrcaSlicer's own
677	   `print_config_def` and its config option classes. JusPrin keeps no second
678	   table of types, enum values, ranges, units, or aliases.
679	6. Search and read cover every setting definition that applies to the
680	   requested scope. Writing is narrower: each scope has its own reviewed
681	   allowlist of keys that may be changed. Every record returned by search or
682	   read says whether the key is writable. Trying to change any other key
683	   returns `unsupported_setting_mutation`. Add a key to an allowlist only
684	   after tests against the real workspace adapter cover, for that scope: the
685	   option type, how dependent settings behave, the visible update in the UI,
686	   the dirty state, saving, and undo or revert.
687	7. A batch is applied completely or not at all. It goes through
688	   `Tab::load_config`, or through the code that already owns that scope.
689	   Never change a config behind the visible preset UI and then imitate the
690	   notifications the UI would have sent.
691	8. Edits to process, filament, and printer presets are not in project Undo.
692	   Their results say `projectUndo: false` and return the previous values, so
693	   that a caller can propose a change that reverses the edit. Object
694	   overrides use one OrcaSlicer snapshot, and their results say
695	   `projectUndo: true`.
696	9. Every result repeats the validated `scope`, and gives the `presetName` of
697	   the preset the settings belong to (for an object, the process preset),
698	   the `sessionId`, and the `revision`. An apply also returns `savedAs`,
699	   which is the name it saved under or empty, and `presetDirty`.
700	10. When a preview finds invalid settings, the call still succeeds, with
701	   `valid: false`. Malformed input is a tool error.
702	11. In JSON, every value is a string in OrcaSlicer's canonical serialization.
703	   Callers may send numbers or booleans, and the decoder converts them.
704	   Every OrcaSlicer id is also a string in JSON.
705	
706	This schema change breaks old callers on purpose. The interface does not need
707	a backward-compatibility period. Update the in-app adapter, the MCP
708	projection, the deterministic agent, the fixtures, and the eval prompts in
709	the same change. Do not add a protocol-version branch, a feature flag, an
710	alias, a fallback, or a migration path for the old forms, in which the scope
711	was missing or the object was implicit. After the change, every caller must
712	send the new contract.
713	
714	### Scope-specific ownership
715	
716	- **Process.** The settings belong to the active
717	  `prints.get_edited_preset()` and are changed through
718	  `Tab(Preset::TYPE_PRINT)`. The rules below continue to apply as
719	  implemented: the normalizer, validation, dirty state, binding an apply to
720	  its preview, and reversing a change with an inverse patch.
721	- **Object.** The settings are the `ModelConfig` of the selected
722	  `ModelObject`. The object is identified only by `target.objectId`. The
723	  project Undo behavior described below continues to apply as implemented.
724	- **Filament or printer, when the target is the preset being edited** (the
725	  one selected in its collection). The tool works on the preset's edited
726	  copy, through its `Tab`, as for the process. Reads include the preset's
727	  unsaved edits.
728	- **Filament, when the target is another preset.** The preset must be in one
729	  of the project's slots; otherwise the call fails with `not_in_project`. It
730	  can be changed only by saving, so a call without `persistAs` fails with
731	  `not_selected`. Apply opens the preset in the filament tab the way the
732	  sidebar's edit button does: `Tab::select_preset`, then `set_filament_idx`
733	  for its slot. Apply then loads the change and saves it through the tab. If
734	  the filament that is open in the tab has unsaved edits, that switch would
735	  either discard them or show a prompt. So preview refuses with
736	  `unsaved_edits`.
737	- **Printer, when the target is another preset.** This is a saved printer
738	  that the project does not use. It can only be saved in place. The write
739	  goes through `Printers::write_unselected_printer`, which is the write
740	  `change_named_printer_nozzle` already makes: it stores the difference from
741	  the parent preset and queues the change for the cloud. Saving a copy of it
742	  would quietly create a second printer that the project does not know
743	  about. So a different `persistAs` fails with `not_selected`.
744	- The printer allowlist (`writable_printer_setting`) contains custom g-code,
745	  printable height, layer-height limits, Z offset, retraction and machine
746	  limits. It leaves out the keys that decide which filament and process fit,
747	  or how many extruders there are: bed shape, nozzle size and type, extruder
748	  count, and printer model. Those change with `printer_setup` or
749	  `printer_change`. The filament allowlist (`writable_filament_setting`)
750	  contains temperatures, cooling, flow, pressure advance, volumetric speed,
751	  density, cost and custom g-code.
752	- Some settings hold one value per extruder or per nozzle kind. Such a
753	  setting keeps its length. A patch with a different number of values fails
754	  with `invalid_setting_value`, because a shorter list would drop the rest.
755	
756	`persistAs` is not valid for `object`. For the preset scopes it works like
757	OrcaSlicer's Save with the name typed in:
758	
759	- The preset's own name overwrites the preset. If OrcaSlicer ships that
760	  preset, the call fails with `read_only_preset`, and the suggestion is
761	  `"<name> - Copy"`, the name SavePresetDialog offers.
762	- Another name that no preset has saves a copy, and the copy takes the
763	  original's place. For a filament, that happens in every project slot that
764	  used the original (`Sidebar::update_presets_from_to`).
765	- A name that another preset has fails with `name_taken`.
766	- A name that SavePresetDialog would refuse fails with
767	  `invalid_preset_name`.
768	
769	Saving the preset that is being edited also saves its other unsaved edits, as
770	Save does. Preview warns about this with `saves_unsaved_edits` and lists
771	those edits. The card's title says where the change is saved ("; save it", or
772	"; save as \"<name>\""). Without `persistAs`, the tool changes only the
773	edited preset and leaves it dirty.
774	
775	In three cases the filament or printer tab would open a dialog. Preview
776	refuses these cases:
777	
778	- a max volumetric speed below 0.5
779	  (`ConfigManipulation::check_filament_max_volumetric_speed`);
780	- a first-layer temperature that is further from the other layers'
781	  temperature than `Tab::validate_filament_temperature_pairs` allows when
782	  saving;
783	- firmware retraction with a wipe that retracts less than 100% first
784	  (`TabPrinter::toggle_options`).
785	
786	### Scope expansion acceptance criteria
787	
788	- The registry offers the same required `scope` enum and the same target
789	  shape through the in-app adapter and the MCP adapter. Catalog tests pin
790	  both projections.
791	- Argument tests reject an omitted or unknown scope, and every target that is
792	  missing, extra, zero-based, mixed, or malformed. No test accepts the old
793	  call shape.
794	- Search, get, preview, and apply are each covered against the fake and the
795	  real workspace adapter, for all four scopes, including a key that can be
796	  read but not written.
797	- Filament tests cover three cases: a preset in a slot that is not open in
798	  its tab, a copy taking the original's slot, and a dirty preset that cannot
799	  be changed without an implicit switch or discard.
800	- Printer tests prove that changing a normal writable value updates the
801	  native field, the dirty marker, the slice invalidation, and the value read
802	  back. They also prove that the topology keys and the compatibility keys
803	  stay unwritable.
804	- Apply tests prove four things: a failed apply changes nothing, the activity
805	  text is right for each scope, a preset change can be reverted or reversed
806	  with an inverse patch, and project Undo applies only to object overrides.
807	- Evals and the deterministic agent's fixtures use explicit scopes before the
808	  old schema is removed. There is no phase in which both schemas are
809	  accepted.
810	
811	### Error codes
812	
813	| Condition | Code |
814	|---|---|
815	| missing or unknown `scope`; forbidden, missing, or malformed `target`; `persistAs` for an object | `invalid_arguments` |
816	| no visible preset of that scope has the target's name | `unknown_preset` with suggestions |
817	| a filament or printer preset that is not being edited, without `persistAs`, or a copy of a printer not in use | `not_selected` |
818	| a filament that is in none of the project's slots, changed by name | `not_in_project` |
819	| `persistAs` overwriting a preset Orca ships | `read_only_preset`, suggesting `"<name> - Copy"` |
820	| `persistAs` naming another existing preset | `name_taken` |
821	| `persistAs` SavePresetDialog would refuse | `invalid_preset_name` |
822	| key not in the definition table | `unknown_setting` with suggestions |
823	| known key not applicable to the requested scope | `unsupported_scope` |
824	| readable key outside that scope's allowlist | `unsupported_setting_mutation` |
825	| requested object is gone, or no FFF printer or process is selected | `workspace_unavailable` |
826	| opening a filament in its tab would discard another dirty edited preset | `unsaved_edits` |
827	| parse failure, bound violation, or layer height outside the printer's range | `invalid_setting_value` with `allowed` or bounds |
828	| a scope-specific dependency or validator rule conflicts | `incompatible_settings` with the conflicting keys |
829	| session, revision, target mapping, preset, or before value changed since preview | `stale_workspace` with expected and current |
830	| client cancelled or the app closed | `cancelled` |
831	| the batch call failed after validation | `execution_failed` |
832	
833	Preview never fails because of what the patch contains. It reports the
834	problem in its result. Apply fails with the first blocking code and changes
835	nothing. Never turn an invariant failure into a success.
836	
837	### Orca entry points the tools use
838	
839	- **Applying a batch of process changes atomically.**
840	  `Tab::load_config(const DynamicPrintConfig&)` in `src/slic3r/GUI/Tab.cpp`
841	  compares the given config with the edited preset and sets every key that
842	  changed. It then runs `update_dirty()`, `reload_config()`, and `update()`
843	  once. `TabPrint::update()` runs the FFF normalizer and reaches
844	  `Plater::on_config_change`, which invalidates slicing the way a sidebar
845	  edit would. So an apply does this: build a config that holds only the
846	  changed keys, then call
847	  `wxGetApp().get_tab(Preset::TYPE_PRINT)->load_config(diff)`.
848	- **Batches of filament and printer changes.** These use the same
849	  `Tab::load_config`, on `Preset::TYPE_FILAMENT` or `Preset::TYPE_PRINTER`.
850	  Before that, preview must model that tab's dependencies, its consequences
851	  for compatibility, and the conditions under which it would open a dialog.
852	  A scope is not complete until a test against the real workspace adapter
853	  proves the native fields, the dirty marker, the slicing invalidation, and
854	  the values read back.
855	- **Parsing.** Clone the config for the scope and call
856	  `set_deserialize(key, text)` for each key. OrcaSlicer throws for an unknown
857	  key and for a value it cannot parse. The canonical value is
858	  `option->serialize()` after parsing.
859	- **Bounds and enums.** These come from `ConfigOptionDef` in
860	  `src/libslic3r/Config.hpp` (`type`, `label`, `category`, `tooltip`,
861	  `sidetext`, `min`, `max`, `mode`, `readonly`, `enum_values`,
862	  `enum_labels`). Treat `min` and `max` as absent when they are the float
863	  limits.
864	- **Validation.** Build the full configuration that would be in effect, with
865	  the cloned config for the scope put in place. Then run the validator that
866	  belongs to that owner. Process and object continue to use
867	  `Slic3r::validate(const FullPrintConfig&)`. Do not assume that process
868	  normalization covers the dependencies of filament or printer settings.
869	- **Dirty state.** Use the APIs of the `PresetCollection` that holds the
870	  preset: the one for dirty state and the one for the difference from the
871	  parent. The result must name the preset and say whether it is dirty after
872	  the call.
873	
874	### The process normalizer can open dialogs and rewrite values
875	
876	The normalizer is two functions in
877	`src/slic3r/GUI/ConfigManipulation.cpp`: `update_print_fff_config` and
878	`toggle_print_fff_options`. They run inside `TabPrint::update()` after every
879	batch. They evaluate every rule against the whole config as it stands after
880	the batch, not only against the keys that changed. Some rules open a modal
881	dialog and then rewrite a value. Other rules rewrite a value without telling
882	anyone. Both are a problem for a tool. A modal dialog opened while a tool is
883	executing blocks the GUI thread while the request waits. A silent rewrite
884	makes the tool's result wrong unless the rewrite is reported.
885	
886	The tools deal with this in two ways.
887	
888	First, preview evaluates the same rules against a clone of the config, using
889	the printer preset and the filament count that the adapter can read. A rule
890	that fires because of a value that was already there is therefore reported
891	too.
892	
893	Second, the two kinds of rule are reported differently. A rule that would
894	open a dialog is a blocking issue. A rule that rewrites silently is a warning
895	that names the dependent key and its predicted value
896	(`normalized_dependency`). Apply then lists the actual rewrite under
897	`normalized`.
898	
899	Preview does not copy OrcaSlicer's option tables. It runs OrcaSlicer's own
900	`ConfigManipulation` on the clone, with no presentation callbacks.
901	
902	The table lists the rules that the current allowlist can reach, as audited
903	when the tools were built. Line numbers drift, so search for the condition
904	text.
905	
906	| Rule in Orca | Reached by | Effect | Preview must |
907	|---|---|---|---|
908	| `layer_height` at or below epsilon | `layer_height` | modal, reset to 0.2 | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the minimum |
909	| `layer_height` above the printer's `max_layer_height` when that exceeds 0.2 | `layer_height` | modal, clamp | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the printer's maximum |
910	| `seam_slope_type` not `None` and absolute `seam_slope_start_height` at or above `layer_height` | lowering `layer_height` | modal, start height reset to 0 | refuse with `incompatible_settings`; evaluate percent values through `get_abs_value`, 100% or above also trips it |
911	| `spiral_mode` on and not all of `wall_loops` 1, `top_shell_layers` 0, `sparse_infill_density` 0 | those three keys | yes/no dialog, several keys rewritten either way | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `spiral_mode` |
912	| `sparse_infill_pattern` without multiline support while `fill_multiline` is above 1 | `sparse_infill_pattern` | silent: `fill_multiline` reset to 1 | predict and report as `normalized_dependency` |
913	| support-gap rounding block | none; it is inside `#if 0` | inactive | do not predict a change that does not happen |
914	| `support_style` not in the set for the support type (normal: default, grid, snug; tree: default, tree_slim, tree_strong, tree_hybrid, organic) | `enable_support`, `support_type`, `support_style` | silent: style reset to default | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the fitting styles in `allowed`; the patch is fixed by the caller, not rewritten |
915	| global `enable_support` while `detect_overhang_wall` is off | `enable_support` | silent: `detect_overhang_wall` turned on, once per query state | predict and report as `normalized_dependency` |
916	| `spiral_mode` on with support or thin walls | `enable_support`, `detect_thin_wall` | yes/no dialog | refuse with `incompatible_settings` (the spiral row above) |
917	| fuzzy skin in an Extrusion or Combined mode without Arachne | `wall_generator` set to classic | yes/no dialog | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `fuzzy_skin_mode` |
918	| `Tab::on_value_change` for `support_type` in simple mode (style reset) and for the support filaments (dialogs) | none: `Tab::load_config` never calls `on_value_change`, and the filament keys are not writable | inactive for tools | nothing |
919	| `toggle_print_fff_options` writes (`enable_arc_fitting`, the slope segment length, `fill_multiline`, `overhang_reverse_threshold`) | none of the new keys directly; the prediction runs the real pass on the clone | silent | report whatever the clone shows |
920	
921	No rule in either function reads the brim, skirt, seam, speed, surface-pattern, interface, contact-distance, threshold or shell-thickness keys, except to enable or disable those keys' own fields. The audit covered both functions and `on_value_change` in `Tab.cpp`, on 2026-09-16. Open-enum keys (the interface layer counts) carry no `allowed` list. Their enum values are shortcuts, and any number in bounds is accepted. A boolean has no numeric bounds.
922	
923	Preview must check every condition that can currently open a dialog. That
924	includes values that were already invalid before the patch: ironing spacing,
925	first-layer height, XY and elephant-foot compensation, alternate-extra-wall,
926	infill-lock depth, and fuzzy-skin settings. Spiral mode also checks support,
927	enforced support layers, thin walls, overhang reversal, timelapse, and
928	wrapping detection.
929	
930	The test against the real workspace adapter asserts two things. First, no
931	top-level dialog appears during apply, for any allowlisted key, under any row
932	above. For the support, brim and style checks, the test applies a
933	tree-support patch with the support page shown and reads the native fields
934	back. Second, every silent rewrite that preview predicted appears in the
935	result with its actual value.
936	
937	If someone later finds a rule that a tool can trigger, that is a defect in
938	the preview. It is not behavior to accept. Adding a key to the allowlist
939	means reading both functions again for every place that reads the key, and
940	extending this table.
941	
942	### Apply binds the previewed values
943	
944	A settings change is previewed three times.
945	
946	1. The client previews and sees the values before and after.
947	2. When the coordinator queues the action, it previews again on the GUI
948	   thread. An invalid patch therefore fails at once. The coordinator stores
949	   that result as the previewed set, and the activity title names the keys
950	   from it.
951	3. At execution, the adapter previews a third time, against the config as it
952	   is at that moment. It compares every "before" value with the previewed
953	   set. A value that has moved is `stale_workspace`. A blocking issue is
954	   `invalid_settings`. In both cases nothing is changed.
955	
956	"Before" values supplied by the client are never trusted. Sometimes
957	OrcaSlicer normalizes a value differently from the preview. In that case the
958	result returns the actual value and lists the key under `normalized`. The
959	change did happen, so the call is a success, and the result says truthfully
960	what happened.
961	
962	### Per-object overrides
963	
964	A read with `scope: "object"` and `target: {"objectId": "..."}` returns the
965	value the object prints with. That is the object's own override where its
966	`ModelConfig` has one (`overridden: true`), and the process value otherwise.
967	
968	A patch is checked against the process config with the object's overrides and
969	the patch applied on top. The checks are the same as for a process patch:
970	parsing, bounds, the conditions that would open a dialog, the support style
971	rule, and `Slic3r::validate`. A key that is neither a `PrintRegionConfig`
972	option nor a `PrintObjectConfig` option is refused with `unsupported_scope`.
973	That is ObjectList's own list for a whole object. No dependencies are
974	predicted. OrcaSlicer runs the normalizer only on the process preset and on
975	edits made in the object settings panel, so an override is stored as written.
976	
977	Apply does the following:
978	
979	1. takes one `Plater::TakeSnapshot` ("Change object settings");
980	2. writes each key with `ModelConfig::set_key_value`;
981	3. calls `ObjectList::object_config_options_changed`, so that the list shows
982	   the settings item;
983	4. calls `Plater::changed_object`, so that the slicing of that object is
984	   invalidated.
985	
986	The result says `projectUndo: true`, and project Undo removes the override.
987	The activity names the object. The coordinator looks the object up in the
988	current snapshot twice, when the action is queued and when it executes, and
989	fails with `missing_object` when the object is gone. The adapter treats a
990	missing target as a broken precondition. No value in a patch removes an
991	override. Only Undo, or the object settings panel, does.
992	
993	### Registry facts worth knowing
994	
995	- `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute` dispatches on `ToolHandler`, with one
996	  explicit block of code per tool. Add a block for each new tool. Do not
997	  replace the blocks with a generic dispatch table.
998	- `kInvalidatingReasons` is the mask of change reasons that make most queued
999	  actions stale. It includes `Settings`, so a queued action fails with
1000	  `stale_revision` when the user edits a setting in the GUI.
1001	  `settings_apply_patch` has its own mask, `Settings | Project`. The reason
1002	  is something the M5 live eval showed: an agent annotated a region between
1003	  its settings preview and its apply, and that model edit (and the slicing
1004	  events after it) made every apply stale. A settings patch is already bound
1005	  to the "before" values it previewed, and the apply checks those values
1006	  again. So its `expectedRevision` only has to be no older than the last
1007	  settings or project change. Model edits do not matter.
1008	- `ToolRegistry::validate_output` accepts only these schema keywords: `type`,
1009	  `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `minimum`,
1010	  `maxItems`, `enum`, `maxLength`. Any other keyword throws. Before using a
1011	  new keyword, extend the validator and add a test. `enum` is checked
1012	  whatever the value's type. `maxLength` counts UTF-8 bytes, which matches
1013	  the byte bounds this registry states everywhere else.
1014	
1015	### Upstream seams the tool system owns
1016	
1017	The tool system has made these changes to files OrcaSlicer owns:
1018	
1019	- `src/CMakeLists.txt`: two added lines.
1020	- `src/dev-utils/platform/unix/build_linux_image.sh.in`: eight added lines.
1021	- `Plater::on_config_change`: one additive call at the end,
1022	  `notify_project_state_changed(ProjectStateChangeReason::Settings)`.
1023	- `GUI_Utils.hpp`: one added declaration, and two lines at the top of
1024	  `DPIAware::ShowModal` (`answer_modal`, which is defined in fork code). If
1025	  upstream changes that function, keep both.
1026	- `Plater::priv::load_files`: a `FileLoadScope` as its first line, and a call
1027	  after `load_config_model` that marks the settings that were actually
1028	  applied.
1029	- The file-open entry points: a `FileOpenScope`, so that choices made before
1030	  loading begins are included.
1031	- `Plater::load_project`: the two model metadata resets at its start were
1032	  moved below its cancelable checks, so that an aborted open leaves the
1033	  project intact. On a rebase, carry those resets to that later point.
1034	- `FileLoads.hpp` is reached through `ProjectState.hpp`, a neutral
1035	  forwarding header.
1036	- `libslic3r/Orient.hpp` and `.cpp`: a new function `score_orientations`,
1037	  added beside `orient()`. It reuses `AutoOrienter` and duplicates the five
1038	  lines of `process()` that build OrcaSlicer's candidate set.
1039	
1040	A warning about `Orient.cpp`. Current upstream (72774e5398) reworks it for
1041	cooling-fan orientation and removes `OrientParamsArea`, which the adapter
1042	copies from today's `OrientJob`. The text merges cleanly. But at that rebase,
1043	`score_orientations` must be checked again against the new `AutoOrienter`,
1044	and the adapter must build its parameters the way the new `OrientJob` does.
1045	
1046	`Plater.cpp` is the fork's busiest file. When `Plater::on_config_change`
1047	changes upstream, the natural resolution is "keep both". No line in
1048	`Tab.cpp`, `ConfigManipulation.cpp`, or `PrintConfig.cpp` changes. The
1049	normalizer hazards are handled in fork-owned code, by refusing the inputs
1050	that would trigger them.
1051	
1052	## Proportional security growth
1053	
1054	Security measures should grow as the server is allowed to do more. Today the server starts automatically, listens only on the numeric loopback address, validates browser origins, and enforces request limits. It has no bearer authentication and no confirmation for each call. Any local process that can reach the socket can execute the offered tools, including mutations and the validated file operations. Origin validation protects against web pages in a browser. It does not identify local processes. Never make this endpoint reachable beyond loopback.
1055	
1056	Review the security design again before adding any of these: remote access, grants that last across restarts, more than one permission level, camera data, upload to a printer, or starting a physical print. At that point, evaluate authenticated pairing, durable credential storage, scopes per client, revocation, rate controls, a privacy review, and a dedicated audit log.
1057	
1058	Paths supplied by a caller stay tightly restricted. `project_open` and `object_import_file` accept absolute paths that can be read. `export_file` requires the expected extension, a parent directory that already exists, and an explicit `overwrite` flag to replace a file. It refuses OrcaSlicer's data directory and its temporary project directories. `project_attachment_read` accepts only an attachment ID, which it resolves inside the project attachment directory. These restrictions limit accidental damage. They do not replace authenticating local clients.
1059	
1060	## Verification commands and limits of current evidence
1061	
1062	From the repository root on the existing macOS development build:
1063	
1064	```sh
1065	cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo --target OrcaSlicer agent_bridge_tests shell_integration_harness -- -j6
1066	build/arm64/tests/agent/RelWithDebInfo/agent_bridge_tests.app/Contents/MacOS/agent_bridge_tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions
1067	python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/mcp -v

4. An edit at the same time: the user changes a setting in the GUI before an external agent's apply executes. The apply fails as stale, and the agent recovers with one preview and one apply. Applies to every toolset.
5. Measuring the load: for the full catalog, the live regression test reports definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for each request, and the transcript is reviewed for cases where the model selected the wrong tool. These numbers decide whether deferral is adopted.

## Settings tools: contract and hazards

The settings tools are the worked example of everything in this guide. This
section records the parts of their design that stay true now that the work is
done. The implementation handoff that produced them is retired. Read this
section again before you add keys to a write allowlist (the list of settings
a tool may change), and before you add any tool that changes a preset.

### Standing decisions

1. Settings are data. There are four generic tools that work on searchable
   records. There is never one tool per setting.
2. Every settings call requires `scope`. Its enum is exactly `process`,
   `object`, `filament`, or `printer`. A call without `scope` fails with
   `invalid_arguments`. There is no default, the scope is never inferred from
   `target`, and there is no alias and no compatibility mode.
3. What `target` must be depends on the scope, and no other forms are
   accepted:

   | `scope` | `target` | Meaning |
   |---|---|---|
   | `process` | forbidden | the active edited FFF process preset |
   | `object` | required `{objectId}` | that object's `ModelConfig` overrides |
   | `filament` | required `{preset}` | that filament preset, by name |
   | `printer` | required `{preset}` | that printer preset, by name |

   These rules apply to `settings_search`, `settings_get`,
   `settings_preview_patch`, and `settings_apply_patch`. A target that is
   extra, missing, empty, or of the wrong shape fails with
   `invalid_arguments`.

   A preset is named the way OrcaSlicer keys it: by its name, which is unique
   within its own collection. `Preset.hpp` says: "The preset name shall be
   unique across a single PresetCollection". Never name a preset by the label
   a menu shows. The header shows a stock printer's model, and
   `Preset::label` puts `"* "` in front of a preset with unsaved edits. Never
   name a preset by an alias either. If no visible preset has the given name,
   the call fails with `unknown_preset`, and the suggestions are the
   project's filaments or the printer in use.

   History: the first draft of this contract named a filament by its 1-based
   project slot, and edited only the selected printer. On 2026-09-29 Kenneth
   chose the preset's name for both. With names, a chat opened for one preset
   can change that preset, and a saved printer the project does not use can
   be changed, without selecting anything first.
4. The scope says which preset or object the settings belong to. It does not
   select anything. `printer_setup` remains the only tool that picks the
   project's printer, process, or filament. A settings call never discards
   dirty edits, never changes nozzle topology (how many nozzles there are and
   of what kind), and never substitutes a compatible profile. A settings call
   selects a preset only in the two places where OrcaSlicer's own Save or
   edit code does. First, a copy saved with `persistAs` takes the original's
   place. Second, a filament that is not the one open in its tab is opened
   there, the way the sidebar's edit button opens it
   (`PlaterPresetComboBox::switch_to_tab`).
5. Metadata, parsing, and serialization all come from OrcaSlicer's own
   `print_config_def` and its config option classes. JusPrin keeps no second
   table of types, enum values, ranges, units, or aliases.
6. Search and read cover every setting definition that applies to the
   requested scope. Writing is narrower: each scope has its own reviewed
   allowlist of keys that may be changed. Every record returned by search or
   read says whether the key is writable. Trying to change any other key
   returns `unsupported_setting_mutation`. Add a key to an allowlist only
   after tests against the real workspace adapter cover, for that scope: the
   option type, how dependent settings behave, the visible update in the UI,
   the dirty state, saving, and undo or revert.
7. A batch is applied completely or not at all. It goes through
   `Tab::load_config`, or through the code that already owns that scope.
   Never change a config behind the visible preset UI and then imitate the
   notifications the UI would have sent.
8. Edits to process, filament, and printer presets are not in project Undo.
   Their results say `projectUndo: false` and return the previous values, so
   that a caller can propose a change that reverses the edit. Object
   overrides use one OrcaSlicer snapshot, and their results say
   `projectUndo: true`.
9. Every result repeats the validated `scope`, and gives the `presetName` of
   the preset the settings belong to (for an object, the process preset),
   the `sessionId`, and the `revision`. An apply also returns `savedAs`,
   which is the name it saved under or empty, and `presetDirty`.
10. When a preview finds invalid settings, the call still succeeds, with
   `valid: false`. Malformed input is a tool error.
11. In JSON, every value is a string in OrcaSlicer's canonical serialization.
   Callers may send numbers or booleans, and the decoder converts them.
   Every OrcaSlicer id is also a string in JSON.

This schema change breaks old callers on purpose. The interface does not need
a backward-compatibility period. Update the in-app adapter, the MCP
projection, the deterministic agent, the fixtures, and the eval prompts in
the same change. Do not add a protocol-version branch, a feature flag, an
alias, a fallback, or a migration path for the old forms, in which the scope
was missing or the object was implicit. After the change, every caller must
send the new contract.

### Scope-specific ownership

- **Process.** The settings belong to the active
  `prints.get_edited_preset()` and are changed through
  `Tab(Preset::TYPE_PRINT)`. The rules below continue to apply as
  implemented: the normalizer, validation, dirty state, binding an apply to
  its preview, and reversing a change with an inverse patch.
- **Object.** The settings are the `ModelConfig` of the selected
  `ModelObject`. The object is identified only by `target.objectId`. The
  project Undo behavior described below continues to apply as implemented.
- **Filament or printer, when the target is the preset being edited** (the
  one selected in its collection). The tool works on the preset's edited
  copy, through its `Tab`, as for the process. Reads include the preset's
  unsaved edits.
- **Filament, when the target is another preset.** The preset must be in one
  of the project's slots; otherwise the call fails with `not_in_project`. It
  can be changed only by saving, so a call without `persistAs` fails with
  `not_selected`. Apply opens the preset in the filament tab the way the
  sidebar's edit button does: `Tab::select_preset`, then `set_filament_idx`
  for its slot. Apply then loads the change and saves it through the tab. If
  the filament that is open in the tab has unsaved edits, that switch would
  either discard them or show a prompt. So preview refuses with
  `unsaved_edits`.
- **Printer, when the target is another preset.** This is a saved printer
  that the project does not use. It can only be saved in place. The write
  goes through `Printers::write_unselected_printer`, which is the write
  `change_named_printer_nozzle` already makes: it stores the difference from
  the parent preset and queues the change for the cloud. Saving a copy of it
  would quietly create a second printer that the project does not know
  about. So a different `persistAs` fails with `not_selected`.
- The printer allowlist (`writable_printer_setting`) contains custom g-code,
  printable height, layer-height limits, Z offset, retraction and machine
  limits. It leaves out the keys that decide which filament and process fit,
  or how many extruders there are: bed shape, nozzle size and type, extruder
  count, and printer model. Those change with `printer_setup` or
  `printer_change`. The filament allowlist (`writable_filament_setting`)
  contains temperatures, cooling, flow, pressure advance, volumetric speed,
  density, cost and custom g-code.
- Some settings hold one value per extruder or per nozzle kind. Such a
  setting keeps its length. A patch with a different number of values fails
  with `invalid_setting_value`, because a shorter list would drop the rest.

`persistAs` is not valid for `object`. For the preset scopes it works like
OrcaSlicer's Save with the name typed in:

- The preset's own name overwrites the preset. If OrcaSlicer ships that
  preset, the call fails with `read_only_preset`, and the suggestion is
  `"<name> - Copy"`, the name SavePresetDialog offers.
- Another name that no preset has saves a copy, and the copy takes the
  original's place. For a filament, that happens in every project slot that
  used the original (`Sidebar::update_presets_from_to`).
- A name that another preset has fails with `name_taken`.
- A name that SavePresetDialog would refuse fails with
  `invalid_preset_name`.

Saving the preset that is being edited also saves its other unsaved edits, as
Save does. Preview warns about this with `saves_unsaved_edits` and lists
those edits. The card's title says where the change is saved ("; save it", or
"; save as \"<name>\""). Without `persistAs`, the tool changes only the
edited preset and leaves it dirty.

In three cases the filament or printer tab would open a dialog. Preview
refuses these cases:

- a max volumetric speed below 0.5
  (`ConfigManipulation::check_filament_max_volumetric_speed`);
- a first-layer temperature that is further from the other layers'
  temperature than `Tab::validate_filament_temperature_pairs` allows when
  saving;
- firmware retraction with a wipe that retracts less than 100% first
  (`TabPrinter::toggle_options`).

### Scope expansion acceptance criteria

- The registry offers the same required `scope` enum and the same target
  shape through the in-app adapter and the MCP adapter. Catalog tests pin
  both projections.
- Argument tests reject an omitted or unknown scope, and every target that is
  missing, extra, zero-based, mixed, or malformed. No test accepts the old
  call shape.
- Search, get, preview, and apply are each covered against the fake and the
  real workspace adapter, for all four scopes, including a key that can be
  read but not written.
- Filament tests cover three cases: a preset in a slot that is not open in
  its tab, a copy taking the original's slot, and a dirty preset that cannot
  be changed without an implicit switch or discard.
- Printer tests prove that changing a normal writable value updates the
  native field, the dirty marker, the slice invalidation, and the value read
  back. They also prove that the topology keys and the compatibility keys
  stay unwritable.
- Apply tests prove four things: a failed apply changes nothing, the activity
  text is right for each scope, a preset change can be reverted or reversed
  with an inverse patch, and project Undo applies only to object overrides.
- Evals and the deterministic agent's fixtures use explicit scopes before the
  old schema is removed. There is no phase in which both schemas are
  accepted.

### Error codes

| Condition | Code |
|---|---|
| missing or unknown `scope`; forbidden, missing, or malformed `target`; `persistAs` for an object | `invalid_arguments` |
| no visible preset of that scope has the target's name | `unknown_preset` with suggestions |
| a filament or printer preset that is not being edited, without `persistAs`, or a copy of a printer not in use | `not_selected` |
| a filament that is in none of the project's slots, changed by name | `not_in_project` |
| `persistAs` overwriting a preset Orca ships | `read_only_preset`, suggesting `"<name> - Copy"` |
| `persistAs` naming another existing preset | `name_taken` |
| `persistAs` SavePresetDialog would refuse | `invalid_preset_name` |
| key not in the definition table | `unknown_setting` with suggestions |
| known key not applicable to the requested scope | `unsupported_scope` |
| readable key outside that scope's allowlist | `unsupported_setting_mutation` |
| requested object is gone, or no FFF printer or process is selected | `workspace_unavailable` |
| opening a filament in its tab would discard another dirty edited preset | `unsaved_edits` |
| parse failure, bound violation, or layer height outside the printer's range | `invalid_setting_value` with `allowed` or bounds |
| a scope-specific dependency or validator rule conflicts | `incompatible_settings` with the conflicting keys |
| session, revision, target mapping, preset, or before value changed since preview | `stale_workspace` with expected and current |
| client cancelled or the app closed | `cancelled` |
| the batch call failed after validation | `execution_failed` |

Preview never fails because of what the patch contains. It reports the
problem in its result. Apply fails with the first blocking code and changes
nothing. Never turn an invariant failure into a success.

### Orca entry points the tools use

- **Applying a batch of process changes atomically.**
  `Tab::load_config(const DynamicPrintConfig&)` in `src/slic3r/GUI/Tab.cpp`
  compares the given config with the edited preset and sets every key that
  changed. It then runs `update_dirty()`, `reload_config()`, and `update()`
  once. `TabPrint::update()` runs the FFF normalizer and reaches
  `Plater::on_config_change`, which invalidates slicing the way a sidebar
  edit would. So an apply does this: build a config that holds only the
  changed keys, then call
  `wxGetApp().get_tab(Preset::TYPE_PRINT)->load_config(diff)`.
- **Batches of filament and printer changes.** These use the same
  `Tab::load_config`, on `Preset::TYPE_FILAMENT` or `Preset::TYPE_PRINTER`.
  Before that, preview must model that tab's dependencies, its consequences
  for compatibility, and the conditions under which it would open a dialog.
  A scope is not complete until a test against the real workspace adapter
  proves the native fields, the dirty marker, the slicing invalidation, and
  the values read back.
- **Parsing.** Clone the config for the scope and call
  `set_deserialize(key, text)` for each key. OrcaSlicer throws for an unknown
  key and for a value it cannot parse. The canonical value is
  `option->serialize()` after parsing.
- **Bounds and enums.** These come from `ConfigOptionDef` in
  `src/libslic3r/Config.hpp` (`type`, `label`, `category`, `tooltip`,
  `sidetext`, `min`, `max`, `mode`, `readonly`, `enum_values`,
  `enum_labels`). Treat `min` and `max` as absent when they are the float
  limits.
- **Validation.** Build the full configuration that would be in effect, with
  the cloned config for the scope put in place. Then run the validator that
  belongs to that owner. Process and object continue to use
  `Slic3r::validate(const FullPrintConfig&)`. Do not assume that process
  normalization covers the dependencies of filament or printer settings.
- **Dirty state.** Use the APIs of the `PresetCollection` that holds the
  preset: the one for dirty state and the one for the difference from the
  parent. The result must name the preset and say whether it is dirty after
  the call.

### The process normalizer can open dialogs and rewrite values

The normalizer is two functions in
`src/slic3r/GUI/ConfigManipulation.cpp`: `update_print_fff_config` and
`toggle_print_fff_options`. They run inside `TabPrint::update()` after every
batch. They evaluate every rule against the whole config as it stands after
the batch, not only against the keys that changed. Some rules open a modal
dialog and then rewrite a value. Other rules rewrite a value without telling
anyone. Both are a problem for a tool. A modal dialog opened while a tool is
executing blocks the GUI thread while the request waits. A silent rewrite
makes the tool's result wrong unless the rewrite is reported.

The tools deal with this in two ways.

First, preview evaluates the same rules against a clone of the config, using
the printer preset and the filament count that the adapter can read. A rule
that fires because of a value that was already there is therefore reported
too.

Second, the two kinds of rule are reported differently. A rule that would
open a dialog is a blocking issue. A rule that rewrites silently is a warning
that names the dependent key and its predicted value
(`normalized_dependency`). Apply then lists the actual rewrite under
`normalized`.

Preview does not copy OrcaSlicer's option tables. It runs OrcaSlicer's own
`ConfigManipulation` on the clone, with no presentation callbacks.

The table lists the rules that the current allowlist can reach, as audited
when the tools were built. Line numbers drift, so search for the condition
text.

| Rule in Orca | Reached by | Effect | Preview must |
|---|---|---|---|
| `layer_height` at or below epsilon | `layer_height` | modal, reset to 0.2 | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the minimum |
| `layer_height` above the printer's `max_layer_height` when that exceeds 0.2 | `layer_height` | modal, clamp | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the printer's maximum |
| `seam_slope_type` not `None` and absolute `seam_slope_start_height` at or above `layer_height` | lowering `layer_height` | modal, start height reset to 0 | refuse with `incompatible_settings`; evaluate percent values through `get_abs_value`, 100% or above also trips it |
| `spiral_mode` on and not all of `wall_loops` 1, `top_shell_layers` 0, `sparse_infill_density` 0 | those three keys | yes/no dialog, several keys rewritten either way | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `spiral_mode` |
| `sparse_infill_pattern` without multiline support while `fill_multiline` is above 1 | `sparse_infill_pattern` | silent: `fill_multiline` reset to 1 | predict and report as `normalized_dependency` |
| support-gap rounding block | none; it is inside `#if 0` | inactive | do not predict a change that does not happen |
| `support_style` not in the set for the support type (normal: default, grid, snug; tree: default, tree_slim, tree_strong, tree_hybrid, organic) | `enable_support`, `support_type`, `support_style` | silent: style reset to default | refuse with `invalid_setting_value` and the fitting styles in `allowed`; the patch is fixed by the caller, not rewritten |
| global `enable_support` while `detect_overhang_wall` is off | `enable_support` | silent: `detect_overhang_wall` turned on, once per query state | predict and report as `normalized_dependency` |
| `spiral_mode` on with support or thin walls | `enable_support`, `detect_thin_wall` | yes/no dialog | refuse with `incompatible_settings` (the spiral row above) |
| fuzzy skin in an Extrusion or Combined mode without Arachne | `wall_generator` set to classic | yes/no dialog | refuse with `incompatible_settings` naming `fuzzy_skin_mode` |
| `Tab::on_value_change` for `support_type` in simple mode (style reset) and for the support filaments (dialogs) | none: `Tab::load_config` never calls `on_value_change`, and the filament keys are not writable | inactive for tools | nothing |
| `toggle_print_fff_options` writes (`enable_arc_fitting`, the slope segment length, `fill_multiline`, `overhang_reverse_threshold`) | none of the new keys directly; the prediction runs the real pass on the clone | silent | report whatever the clone shows |

No rule in either function reads the brim, skirt, seam, speed, surface-pattern, interface, contact-distance, threshold or shell-thickness keys, except to enable or disable those keys' own fields. The audit covered both functions and `on_value_change` in `Tab.cpp`, on 2026-09-16. Open-enum keys (the interface layer counts) carry no `allowed` list. Their enum values are shortcuts, and any number in bounds is accepted. A boolean has no numeric bounds.

Preview must check every condition that can currently open a dialog. That
includes values that were already invalid before the patch: ironing spacing,
first-layer height, XY and elephant-foot compensation, alternate-extra-wall,
infill-lock depth, and fuzzy-skin settings. Spiral mode also checks support,
enforced support layers, thin walls, overhang reversal, timelapse, and
wrapping detection.

The test against the real workspace adapter asserts two things. First, no
top-level dialog appears during apply, for any allowlisted key, under any row
above. For the support, brim and style checks, the test applies a
tree-support patch with the support page shown and reads the native fields
back. Second, every silent rewrite that preview predicted appears in the
result with its actual value.

If someone later finds a rule that a tool can trigger, that is a defect in
the preview. It is not behavior to accept. Adding a key to the allowlist
means reading both functions again for every place that reads the key, and
extending this table.

### Apply binds the previewed values

A settings change is previewed three times.

1. The client previews and sees the values before and after.
2. When the coordinator queues the action, it previews again on the GUI
   thread. An invalid patch therefore fails at once. The coordinator stores
   that result as the previewed set, and the activity title names the keys
   from it.
3. At execution, the adapter previews a third time, against the config as it
   is at that moment. It compares every "before" value with the previewed
   set. A value that has moved is `stale_workspace`. A blocking issue is
   `invalid_settings`. In both cases nothing is changed.

"Before" values supplied by the client are never trusted. Sometimes
OrcaSlicer normalizes a value differently from the preview. In that case the
result returns the actual value and lists the key under `normalized`. The
change did happen, so the call is a success, and the result says truthfully
what happened.

### Per-object overrides

A read with `scope: "object"` and `target: {"objectId": "..."}` returns the
value the object prints with. That is the object's own override where its
`ModelConfig` has one (`overridden: true`), and the process value otherwise.

A patch is checked against the process config with the object's overrides and
the patch applied on top. The checks are the same as for a process patch:
parsing, bounds, the conditions that would open a dialog, the support style
rule, and `Slic3r::validate`. A key that is neither a `PrintRegionConfig`
option nor a `PrintObjectConfig` option is refused with `unsupported_scope`.
That is ObjectList's own list for a whole object. No dependencies are
predicted. OrcaSlicer runs the normalizer only on the process preset and on
edits made in the object settings panel, so an override is stored as written.

Apply does the following:

1. takes one `Plater::TakeSnapshot` ("Change object settings");
2. writes each key with `ModelConfig::set_key_value`;
3. calls `ObjectList::object_config_options_changed`, so that the list shows
   the settings item;
4. calls `Plater::changed_object`, so that the slicing of that object is
   invalidated.

The result says `projectUndo: true`, and project Undo removes the override.
The activity names the object. The coordinator looks the object up in the
current snapshot twice, when the action is queued and when it executes, and
fails with `missing_object` when the object is gone. The adapter treats a
missing target as a broken precondition. No value in a patch removes an
override. Only Undo, or the object settings panel, does.

### Registry facts worth knowing

- `ToolExecutionCoordinator::execute` dispatches on `ToolHandler`, with one
  explicit block of code per tool. Add a block for each new tool. Do not
  replace the blocks with a generic dispatch table.
- `kInvalidatingReasons` is the mask of change reasons that make most queued
  actions stale. It includes `Settings`, so a queued action fails with
  `stale_revision` when the user edits a setting in the GUI.
  `settings_apply_patch` has its own mask, `Settings | Project`. The reason
  is something the M5 live eval showed: an agent annotated a region between
  its settings preview and its apply, and that model edit (and the slicing
  events after it) made every apply stale. A settings patch is already bound
  to the "before" values it previewed, and the apply checks those values
  again. So its `expectedRevision` only has to be no older than the last
  settings or project change. Model edits do not matter.
- `ToolRegistry::validate_output` accepts only these schema keywords: `type`,
  `properties`, `required`, `additionalProperties`, `items`, `minimum`,
  `maxItems`, `enum`, `maxLength`. Any other keyword throws. Before using a
  new keyword, extend the validator and add a test. `enum` is checked
  whatever the value's type. `maxLength` counts UTF-8 bytes, which matches
  the byte bounds this registry states everywhere else.

### Upstream seams the tool system owns

The tool system has made these changes to files OrcaSlicer owns:

- `src/CMakeLists.txt`: two added lines.
- `src/dev-utils/platform/unix/build_linux_image.sh.in`: eight added lines.
- `Plater::on_config_change`: one additive call at the end,
  `notify_project_state_changed(ProjectStateChangeReason::Settings)`.
- `GUI_Utils.hpp`: one added declaration, and two lines at the top of
  `DPIAware::ShowModal` (`answer_modal`, which is defined in fork code). If
  upstream changes that function, keep both.
- `Plater::priv::load_files`: a `FileLoadScope` as its first line, and a call
  after `load_config_model` that marks the settings that were actually
  applied.
- The file-open entry points: a `FileOpenScope`, so that choices made before
  loading begins are included.
- `Plater::load_project`: the two model metadata resets at its start were
  moved below its cancelable checks, so that an aborted open leaves the
  project intact. On a rebase, carry those resets to that later point.
- `FileLoads.hpp` is reached through `ProjectState.hpp`, a neutral
  forwarding header.
- `libslic3r/Orient.hpp` and `.cpp`: a new function `score_orientations`,
  added beside `orient()`. It reuses `AutoOrienter` and duplicates the five
  lines of `process()` that build OrcaSlicer's candidate set.

A warning about `Orient.cpp`. Current upstream (72774e5398) reworks it for
cooling-fan orientation and removes `OrientParamsArea`, which the adapter
copies from today's `OrientJob`. The text merges cleanly. But at that rebase,
`score_orientations` must be checked again against the new `AutoOrienter`,
and the adapter must build its parameters the way the new `OrientJob` does.

`Plater.cpp` is the fork's busiest file. When `Plater::on_config_change`
changes upstream, the natural resolution is "keep both". No line in
`Tab.cpp`, `ConfigManipulation.cpp`, or `PrintConfig.cpp` changes. The
normalizer hazards are handled in fork-owned code, by refusing the inputs
that would trigger them.

## Proportional security growth

Security measures should grow as the server is allowed to do more. Today the server starts automatically, listens only on the numeric loopback address, validates browser origins, and enforces request limits. It has no bearer authentication and no confirmation for each call. Any local process that can reach the socket can execute the offered tools, including mutations and the validated file operations. Origin validation protects against web pages in a browser. It does not identify local processes. Never make this endpoint reachable beyond loopback.

Review the security design again before adding any of these: remote access, grants that last across restarts, more than one permission level, camera data, upload to a printer, or starting a physical print. At that point, evaluate authenticated pairing, durable credential storage, scopes per client, revocation, rate controls, a privacy review, and a dedicated audit log.

Paths supplied by a caller stay tightly restricted. `project_open` and `object_import_file` accept absolute paths that can be read. `export_file` requires the expected extension, a parent directory that already exists, and an explicit `overwrite` flag to replace a file. It refuses OrcaSlicer's data directory and its temporary project directories. `project_attachment_read` accepts only an attachment ID, which it resolves inside the project attachment directory. These restrictions limit accidental damage. They do not replace authenticating local clients.

build/arm64/tests/agent/RelWithDebInfo/agent_bridge_tests.app/Contents/MacOS/agent_bridge_tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/mcp -v

c35dcfcd20 Let the settings tools change supports, adhesion, seam and speeds, and one object's overrides

The write allowlist grows to the support family, brim and skirt, seam
position, the remaining wall, shell and infill keys, and ten speed keys,
each traced through the FFF normalizer, its toggles, and Tab's value
handlers. A support style that does not fit the support type is refused
with the styles that do, instead of being reset silently; booleans no
longer go through the float bounds check; open enums carry no allowed
list.

settings_search takes writable and changedOnly, and several terms in one
query. Unknown keys suggest settings that share their words, writable
ones first.

settings_get, settings_preview_patch and settings_apply_patch take
target.objectId: reads return the object's override where it has one,
patches refuse print-wide keys, and apply writes the object's
ModelConfig as one undo step (projectUndo: true), with the approval card
naming the object. The shell harness applies a tree-support patch with
the Support page shown and a dialog counter installed, reads the native
fields back, and checks the object override, its read-back and its Undo.

4

6	
7	One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**
8	
9	- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
10	- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
11	- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.
12	
13	Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.
14	
15	## The ten principles
16	
17	### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much
18	
19	**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.
20	
21	**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.
22	
23	**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?
24	
25	**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.
26	
27	### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge
28	
29	**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.
30	
31	**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.
32	
33	**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?
34	
35	**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.
36	
37	### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it
38	
39	**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.
40	
41	**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.
42	
43	**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?
44	
45	**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.
46	
47	### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism
48	
49	**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.
50	
51	**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.
52	
53	**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?
54	
55	**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.
56	
57	### 5. One seam beats many touch points
58	
59	**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.
60	
61	**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.
62	
63	**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?
64	
65	**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.
66	
67	### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict
68	
69	**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.
70	
71	**Mechanism.** A conflict is a stop; drift between two copies is silent and unbounded. Trading an invisible risk for a visible, small, recurring one is a good trade.
72	
73	**The test.** Where did the logic I removed actually go? A move has one implementation; only a duplication risks divergence. If I wrote new behavior beside an existing upstream path rather than calling it, upstream's future improvements will never reach our users.
74	
75	**Violation.** Writing a second object-duplication routine next to OrcaSlicer's clipboard path and pointing an existing dialog at it. Reusing the existing path — extending it where it was too narrow — keeps one implementation.
76	
77	### 7. Unavoidable conflicts must be easy to resolve correctly
78	
79	**Rule.** When you must delete or relocate an upstream line, say at the site what moved, where it went, and what a future rebase must carry across.
80	
81	**Mechanism.** The real cost of a conflict is not the stop; it is the chance of resolving it wrongly. Appending near an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — keep both — is right. Deleting an upstream line yields a conflict whose obvious resolution — take mine, the logic moved — silently discards whatever upstream did to that line in the meantime.
82	
83	**The test.** Six months from now, is the natural resolution of the conflict I am creating the correct one? If not, what does the resolver need to read to get it right, and is that text next to the conflict?
84	
85	**Violation.** Removing an upstream snapshot label that upstream later localized. Git stops for a human, but the intent-faithful resolution throws the translation away, and nothing at the site says otherwise.
86	
87	### 8. Do not diverge where you gain nothing; converge where upstream already went
88	
89	**Rule.** No gratuitous formatting, reordering, or whitespace differences. Before reverting a cosmetic difference, compare against current upstream — it may have made the same change.
90	
91	**Mechanism.** Every valueless difference is a conflict site that buys nothing. And if upstream has independently arrived at your version, "fixing" it back creates divergence rather than removing it. Adopting a change upstream has already made converges the two trees early and makes the eventual conflict resolve itself.
92	
93	**The test.** Does this difference carry meaning? Has upstream already made it?
94	
95	**Violation.** Consuming a shared blank line in a list of build subdirectories, where upstream also appends entries.
96	
97	### 9. Verify the risk claim instead of reasoning about it
98	
99	**Rule.** Before asserting that a change is or is not rebase-risky, check it. Three checks, each one command: does git actually conflict there; has upstream already converged on the same change; is the change a move or a duplication.
100	
101	**Mechanism.** A coherent story about fork risk is not a true one, and every one of these is cheaper to check than to argue about. Reasoning alone reliably produces confident, wrong claims — that a lost change is "silent" when git stops for it, that a move is a "duplication," that a cosmetic difference is gratuitous when upstream shares it.
102	
103	**The test.** Did I run the simulation, or am I describing what I expect it to say?
104	
105	**Violation.** A report that lists which files are rebase-sensitive and calls the change narrow, without having run the merge simulation that would have found two lossy resolutions waiting in it.
106	
107	### 10. Pull direction dominates every local edit
108	
109	**Rule.** Replay the fork's own commits onto upstream. Never merge upstream in, and never rebase the whole branch.
110	
111	**Mechanism.** The fork's own footprint is small; the inherited release-branch history is not. 112	
113	**The test.** Am I replaying our commits onto upstream, or bringing upstream into ours?
114	
115	**Violation.** `git merge upstream/main`, which produces a conflict list dominated by vendor profiles, translations, and CI files that JusPrin has never edited.
116	
117	## Before you finish
118	
119	A change that touches upstream-owned files is not done until this is recorded in the handback or pull request:
120	
121	1. **The rebase simulation and its result.** Run it against current upstream and name both endpoint commits — measurements are not reproducible otherwise.
122	
123	   ```bash
124	   git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=<fork base> upstream/main HEAD
125	   ```
126	
127	   For each conflicted file, state whether the natural resolution is correct or lossy. A lossy one is a defect to fix now, not a note for later.
128	
129	2. **An account of every upstream line deleted or rewritten.** Where the logic went, and why an additive form was not possible.
130	
131	3. **A statement of what the fork now owns.** Policy, a neutral seam, or upstream behavior. The third needs an explicit justification.
132	
133	An automatic merge is evidence about today's text. It is not proof that a future rebase will merge, and never proof that the merged result behaves correctly. After every upstream update, run the focused contract tests, the full native build, the real multi-plate workflow, native gizmo input, and the stock-behavior regression checks.
134	
135	## This fork's terrain
136	
137	Facts specific to OrcaSlicer, worth knowing before choosing where to put a seam. They change over time; re-measure rather than trusting these.
138	
139	`Plater.cpp` is by far the busiest file the fork touches, followed by the central `src/slic3r/CMakeLists.txt`, `GLCanvas3D.cpp`, and `PartPlate.cpp`. `GLToolbar` and `GLGizmosManager` are quiet. File-level churn is only a first approximation: some functions inside `Plater.cpp` have not been touched upstream in the entire life of this fork, and a seam there is far cheaper than the file's overall rate suggests. Measure the function, not just the file.
140	
141	Some native state is shared rather than owned by one object. OrcaSlicer's collapse toolbar belongs to `Plater` and is used by both the Prepare and Preview canvases, so a per-canvas guard cannot save and restore it correctly. Shared state needs one owner at the shared lifetime boundary, and exact restoration needs a getter as well as a setter.
142	
143	`MainFrame`'s Notebook is cheaper to wrap than to dismantle. Dozens of
144	upstream predicates — menu and shortcut enabling, `can_delete`, slice status
145	updates, undo/redo gating — key off `m_tabpanel->GetSelection()`, so removing
146	or reparenting the Prepare/Preview pages breaks them with no conflict and no
147	error. A shell gets a tabless full-window layout for free instead: hide the
148	strip via the public `GetBtnsListCtrl()` (wxBookCtrlBase gives a hidden
149	controller zero size, so pages fill the client area), and the stock slice and
150	print side buttons disappear with it because `ButtonsListCtrl` reparents them
151	into the strip at construction. The Phase 1 production shell reached a
152	19-added-line upstream footprint this way where the POC's reparenting shell
153	needed edits across eight upstream files.
154	
155	The same measurement gives the rule for every fork-owned screen that comes
156	after the shell. OrcaSlicer's surfaces (the stock homepage, Prepare, Preview,
157	Monitor, the settings tabs) stay inside the Notebook, because their
158	correctness depends on it. Fork-owned surfaces (the header, the Agent pane,
159	Home, and whatever follows) live outside it, as siblings of the Notebook in a
160	fork-owned sizer, shown and hidden by the shell. The shell *reads* the
161	Notebook's selection to decide what to show and *never edits its page list*:
162	no `RemovePage`, `InsertPage`, or reparenting of a stock page. Removing or
163	replacing a page hands the fork the meaning of that index. Upstream keeps
164	addressing it by number — `tpHome` as a dialog parent, the target of
165	`EVT_LOAD_URL`, the tab `post_init` returns to — and every one of those lands
166	on the fork's widget with no conflict and no error. If a fork surface truly
167	must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.
168	
169	Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
170	screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
171	availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
172	selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
173	Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
174	page, silently.
175	
176	Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
177	function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
178	sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
179	`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
180	and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
181	without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
182	owned by Plater's event handler.
183	
184	Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).

must be a page, append it last, where no upstream code addresses it.

Navigation between screens stays a Notebook selection change even when the
screen being left is fork-owned. Menu and shortcut enabling, undo and redo
availability, and slice-status updates all read `GetSelection()`, so the
selection must remain the one record of which OrcaSlicer surface is active.
Showing Prepare any other way leaves those predicates answering for the wrong
page, silently.

Some stock behavior is already exposed as an event idiom rather than a
function. Upstream itself drives plate slicing from two places with the same
sequence — the slice button and the Cmd+R shortcut both run
`plater->update(true, true)`, post `EVT_GLTOOLBAR_SLICE_PLATE` to the Plater,
and select the Preview tab — so fork code may repeat that short dispatch
without violating the shared-implementation rule; the behavior itself stays
owned by Plater's event handler.

Historical measurements and the incidents behind several of these rules are in the [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md) and, for the spike era, in the [POC reference](poc-reference.md).
